leaks.description: Converted dicts are new plain dicts built in input key order (dict comprehension, main.py:223). When two keys convert to the same key, the key keeps the position of its first occurrence and the last value wins: camelize({'a_b': 1, 'x': 0, 'aB': 2}) == {'aB': 2, 'x': 0} with 'aB' first. Fixtures check the surviving value; parity compares objects order-insensitively (porterlib/parity.py:93), so key order and collision position are NOT checked by fixtures. Port: serde_json with preserve_order, build a fresh Map and insert in order (Map::insert keeps the first position and replaces the value; never Map::remove). Cover order with a Rust unit test.

Anything that is not a list or Mapping goes through the string path: None -> '', bool -> str() then converted (camelize(True) == 'true', pascalize(True) == 'True', dekebabize(False) == 'False'), int/float -> str(). The return type changes: a non-negative int comes back unchanged as an int (camelize(1234) == 1234, tested), a negative int comes back as a string (camelize(-5) == '-5', dekebabize(-5) == '_5'). Predicates follow: is_camelcase(5) is True, is_camelcase(-5), is_camelcase(None), is_camelcase(True) are False. The strategy decides whether the Rust API accepts top-level Null/Bool/Number values (and reproduces this) or rejects them (those fixtures then become declared divergences).

leaks.description: Float inputs are stringified with Python repr before conversion: str(1.0) == '1.0', str(1e16) == '1e+16', str(1e-05) == '1e-05', so camelize(1e-05) == '1e05' (the '-0' is a separator run) and dekebabize(1e-05) == '1e_05'. Rust's {} prints 1 and 10000000000000000 (pair trap T4). Only matters if top-level numbers are accepted. Float dict values pass through untouched; the harness needs serde_json float_roundtrip to read them back exactly.

camelize, pascalize, decamelize and depascalize return the ORIGINAL input when the whitespace-stripped string s is s.isupper() or s.isnumeric(); kebabize and dekebabize only on s.isnumeric(). The original keeps its whitespace: camelize('HELLO WORLD') == 'HELLO WORLD' but kebabize('HELLO WORLD') == 'HELLOWORLD'; camelize('1 2') == '1 2'. str.isupper() means at least one cased character, no Lowercase character and no titlecase (Lt) character: 'ǅ'.isupper() is False, 'Ⅻ'.isupper() is True, 'ª' counts as lowercase. str.isnumeric() means every character has a Unicode Numeric_Type: it includes '½', '²', 'Ⅻ' and 91 Han ideographs such as '三' that are general category Lo, which Rust char::is_numeric (Nd/Nl/No only) misses, so camelize('三 四') == '三 四' needs a Numeric_Type table or the exact list. Empty s is neither.

On the string path every Python \s character is deleted anywhere in the string, keys included (so {'a b': 1, 'ab': 2} collides to {'ab': 2}). Python \s for str is str.isspace(): Unicode White_Space plus U+001C..U+001F (29 code points: 9-D, 1C-1F, 20, 85, A0, 1680, 2000-200A, 2028, 2029, 202F, 205F, 3000). U+200B, U+FEFF and U+180E are not whitespace. deps.json maps this to [\s\x1C-\x1F]+.

Case changes use Python's full Unicode mappings, which can change length: 'ß'.upper() == 'SS', 'ŉ'.upper() == 'ʼN', 'ﬀ'.upper() == 'FF', 'İ'.lower() == 'i̇' (2 code points), 'ᾀ'.upper() == 'ἈΙ'. Whole-string .lower() (decamelize, kebabize) applies Final_Sigma ('ΟδΟΣ' -> 'οδος', but 'ΑΣ.x' -> 'ασ.x'); single-character s[0].lower()/.upper() and the per-match upper() have no context. Titlecase digraphs (ǅ ǈ ǋ ǲ, Greek ᾈ) are neither upper nor lower: camelize('ǅ') == 'ǆ'. Indexing (s[0], s[1:], s[:2], m.group(0)[-1]) is by code point (pair trap T3). Rust char::to_uppercase/to_lowercase are full mappings and str::to_lowercase applies Final_Sigma; std has no titlecase predicate.
leaks.fixtures: tag unicode, generators gen-chars.* and gen-words.*

leaks.description: The regex classes [A-Z] are ASCII only, so words split only before ASCII capitals (decamelize('helloÉcole') == 'helloécole'), while \d is Unicode Nd (Arabic-Indic digits join acronyms: decamelize('fooABC١٢') == 'foo_abc١٢') and isupper/isnumeric/upper/lower/title are Unicode-aware. str.title() on an ACRONYM_RE match restarts after a digit ('MB2X' -> 'Mb2X', 'AB٣C' -> 'Ab٣C'); matches hold only ASCII capitals and Nd digits, so a hand-written title over that alphabet is exact.

Fixtures were recorded with CPython 3.14.6, Unicode 16.0.0. Python \d, isnumeric, isupper, isspace and case mappings follow that table; CPython 3.9-3.13 ship older tables, and the Rust side's answers come from the regex crate's and the toolchain's Unicode tables. A different Unicode version on either side can flip generated unicode cases. Re-record when changing the Python version.

Only dict keys are converted. Strings inside lists are returned as they are: camelize(['a_b', 'cD']) == ['a_b', 'cD'], so is_camelcase(['a_b']) is True. Dict values are never converted, only walked when they are lists or dicts.

Not fixture inputs, because serde_json::Value cannot carry them (chosen: excluded from fixtures and recorded here as known divergences). Python behavior, probed on the pinned source: (1) dicts with non-str keys: int keys >= 0 stay ints, negative int, float, None and tuple keys become strings ('-1', '1.5', '', '(1,2)'), True and 1 are the same key ({True: 1, 1: 2} -> {'true': 2}); (2) tuples and sets are not walked: at top level they are stringified (camelize(('a_b',)) == "('aB',)", camelize({'a_b'}) == "{'aB'}"), inside containers they come back unchanged; every JSON array is walked in Rust; (3) bytes: camelize(b'a_b') == "b'aB'"; (4) Mapping subclasses (OrderedDict, MappingProxyType) come back as plain dict; (5) ints beyond 64 bits: 2**70 unchanged, -2**70 -> '-1180591620717411303424'; (6) NaN and Infinity: 'nan', 'inf', '-inf' ('_inf' for dekebabize); (7) lone surrogates: camelize('a_\ud800') == 'a\ud800', impossible in a Rust String.

The key walker recurses once per nesting level. CPython raises RecursionError past about 990 levels (default limit 1000; a 3000-level dict fails). A recursive Rust port overflows the stack at a depth that depends on the thread stack size, and that aborts the process instead of returning an error; serde_json's parser stops at depth 128. Fixtures stop at depth 42 (the oracle serializer truncates past 64). The strategy decides the depth guarantee.

free: Helper names and structure (_is_none, _process_keys, _fix_abbreviations, _separate_words) and whether regexes are used at all, as long as the outputs match.
The four regex constants: not public in the crate; compiled once (LazyLock) or not at all.
Module layout: humps.main versus the package root; the crate exposes the ten functions at its root under names the strategy picks (bindings translate the Python call ids).
Object identity: Python returns the very input object on early returns and builds new containers otherwise; the port may return clones or take ownership. The input must not be observably mutated.
Argument and return types (str and serde_json::Value per the user's decision; separate str and Value entry points are fine) and the type stubs.
Error types for inputs the Rust API rejects at compile time or by type (the source raises nothing on JSON input).
